evidence.quote:
This is a well-articulated and well-researched article on the concept of joint controllership in
biomedical research consortia.
Overall, I wholeheartedly agree with both the legal analysis made, and the proposed model of
"funnel" analysis.
One nuance in the literature, however, appears not to have been addressed. Namely, the authors
state that the test for controllership has not changed from the DPD to the GDPR.
My own position is that the liability rules associated to joint controllership have changed between
the DPD and the GDPR.
The DPD recognized a wide 'concept' of joint controller - but limited the potential liability of each
controller to the acts that were associated to their responsibilities within the broader
controllership arrangement.
According to the DPD, the concept of joint controllership was articulated in a broad manner
(capturing a considerable "mix" of different institutional arrangements). However, liability arising
from joint controllership was narrowly construed and associated to the activities left to that
controller's oversight (see e.g. FashionID on this topic).
Conversely, art. 82 of the GDPR establishes the joint and several liability of each joint controller in
a joint controllership arrangement (with further support at Recital 146).
Therefore, it would appear that there is a substantive shift in the structure of the joint and several
liability rules:
Courts have broadly interpreted the concept in the past, but have used the structure of the liability
rule to limit the arising damages.




The GDPR implemented a joint and several liability rule, bringing together both a "broad" legal
framing (jurisprudential) and a broad potential for liability.
I believe that following change might benefit the article:
I. To describe in the review of the history of the DPD and GDPR the shift in liability rule (i.e. that the
DPD had a broad conception of JCs but a narrow conception of liability (each liable only for their
own acts), whereas the GDPR adopts both a broad framing for joint controllership jurisprudentially constructed - and for liability (as constructed through statute).
Otherwise, however, the article is strong as stands and is recommended for indexing.

1. Introduction
First of all, we would like to thank the reviewers for their time and comments. In general,
these are positive. Especially Anne Barth gave comments which should lead to textual
changes. For example, she was completely correct that we forgot a ‘not’ when stating that a
large group of controllers does not add to the protection of the data subjects. In bold the
omission which Bahr showed and in italics what would made the sentence clearer to
reviewer Chen. Given those and other textual comments, we submitted a version 2. This
version does not differ substantially from version 1. The changes are editorial, given the
comments and do not encompass recent care law or literature which we found at after the
submission. Version 2 is, as lawyers would say, ‘ex tunc’, Infra we will discuss what changes
we did not incorporate or only very moderately. However, before doing that, we should
discuss new developments as significant time has passed between the publication of our
paper and this response to the reviewers. Hence, this reply is more ‘ex nunc’. Lastly, our
apologies for the delay in this response. We needed a ‘seasonal break’ to find time for the
update.
1. New developments
There are two. The first is the European Health Data Space (EHDS) proposal by the European
Commission. That very complex proposal and its comments cannot be discussed here. It
also has clauses about ‘joint controllers’. Though the EHDS will be a major game changer
for the secondary use of health data, it claims to adhere to the GDPR with (probably) a new
Union law legal basis in the sense of article 9.2 I and j. Which entities are joint controllers
may be influenced by the EHDS but cannot be decided by the EHDS as that decision follows
from the GDPR. From that perspective it foremost matters whether new case law sheds new
light in the ‘joint controller’ discussion. Obviously, new case law could also influence our
proposal. A recent judgement of the CJEU in case C-683/21[1] does shed new light on this
issue and we should discuss that decision first. That decision is important for a variety of
reasons. We will only highlight the essence of the judgment for the issue under discussion
here and abstain from details about the circumstances or other aspects of the interesting
judgement, relevant for the interpretation of other clauses of the GDPR. That essence is, as
mentioned in number 30 of the judgment, that (our italics added): ……who exerts influence
over the processing of such data, for his, her or its own purposes, and who participates, as a
result, in the determination of the purposes and means of that processing, may be
regarded as a controller in respect of such processing. The CJEU states that its judgment
follows from its earlier decisions. We submit that this is true for a very large extent but that
the line in italics is an important refinement which was more implicit in the earlier decisions
we discussed in our paper. A law firm which is consulted about a certain data processing
also exerts influence as it will give advice on what certainly shouldn’t be done and how it
may be done. But it does not do so for its own purposes regarding the data involved. That
‘influence’ versus ‘own purposes regarding the data involved’ is what we tried to disentangle
in the sieve model. As it is more complicated there than in the just given example of the
externally hired law firm. If a law firm or ICT consultant is embedded in an EU-funded
research consortium as a partner, that partner exerts influence but is also sort of an ally for
the purposes. We will come back to that when we discuss the criticism of the reviewers on
the sieve model.
1. The GDPR and DPD differ on joint controllership
Reviewer Bernier states that joint controllership under the Data Protection Directive (DPD)




and the GDPR differ. In the DPD the responsibilities resulting from joint controllership were
narrowly constructed while under GDPR joint controllership leads to joint and several
liability. It is correct that we did not discuss this issue. However, we note that this does not
affect the strictly legal analysis, as in our paper, of whether a situation is at hand. We
discussed under what conditions parties are considered to be joint controllers, not the
consequences if they are considered joint controllers. We have added a clarification
regarding this point. With present knowledge, it might even be questioned whether the
GDPR brought a major change in this respect. In mentioned judgement the CJEU reiterated
at point 42 that: However, the existence of joint responsibility does not necessarily imply
equal responsibility of the various operators involved in the processing of personal data. On
the contrary, those operators may be involved at different stages of that processing of
personal data and to different degrees, so that the level of responsibility of each of them
must be assessed with regard to all the relevant circumstances of the particular case
(judgment of 5 June 2018, Wirtschaftsakademie Schleswig-Holstein, C‑210/16,
EU:C:2018:388, paragraph 43). So, even though this review led to a question mark, we did
not follow-up on it.
[1] Judgement of December 5 2023, ECLI:EU:C:2023:949
